scenes.title: 재미있는데, 괜찮은 걸까?
lines: Hello, this is Yamyam Coding. A Diablo II hero sweeps through a screen full of monsters, but the way it plays resembles Vampire Survivors.
This is D2 Survivors, an unofficial fan game. Familiar characters create a fresh experience, but does being fun justify using another game’s creative work?
We will examine what makes these games fun, distinguish borrowing game rules from using artwork, and consider how to judge a free fan game.
This question extends beyond D2 Survivors. Vampire Survivors, which popularized this genre, also drew inspiration from an earlier game.

scenes.title: 뱀파이어 서바이버는 원조였을까?
lines: In Vampire Survivors, you primarily control movement. Weapons attack automatically, and defeated enemies leave experience gems to collect.
When the experience bar fills, you level up and choose a weapon or an upgrade. Movement, defeating enemies, collecting experience, and choosing growth form a repeating loop.
The key is not how fast you press an attack button. It is deciding where to move among enemies and which upgrades to combine.

The Korean mobile game Magic Survival demonstrated this kind of play earlier. In an interview about its development, the creator of Vampire Survivors acknowledged playing it and drawing inspiration from it.
The interview described a very similar early prototype. That fact alone, however, does not establish copyright infringement.
We need to distinguish rules and ideas from concrete artwork and sound. To see what experience was built on those rules, let us follow the growth in Vampire Survivors.

scenes.title: 단순한 규칙이 강한 재미가 되는 과정
lines: At first you have few weapons, with large gaps between attacks. When monsters approach, you dodge and position yourself for the next hit.
As levels rise, attack count and range increase, and weapon combinations transform the screen. The character who was fleeing can eventually push back entire hordes.
The controls stay simple, yet the results make your increased strength obvious. That feeling makes the next upgrade inviting.
Weapon and passive-item combinations, weapon evolutions, treasure chests, and character unlocks reinforce the loop. Each choice creates anticipation for the next reward.
The development interview describes prioritizing enjoyable, viable combinations over giving every weapon equal strength in a single-player game.
That does not mean balance never matters. It means becoming overwhelmingly powerful can itself be an intentional part of the experience.
This reveals where D2 Survivors connects with Diablo II. Defeating enemies leads to the next stage of growth.

scenes.title: 디아블로의 익숙함이 더해지면
lines: D2 Survivors combines that loop with Diablo II’s classes, skills, monsters, and items. You can begin with familiar heroes such as the Sorceress or Necromancer.
In combat, you move to evade enemies while skills activate automatically. At level-up, you choose a card to continue building your character.
You also obtain, equip, and sell gear in pursuit of stronger stats. The growth within a run overlaps with the anticipation of loot.
The official site describes seven classes, five acts, and Nightmare and Hell difficulties. Shared names do not mean every stat and combat rule matches the original Diablo II.
That familiarity is powerful for existing fans. A skill name or an item’s appearance can immediately suggest what to collect and what character to build.
It reduces the burden of learning while evoking memories. But those same familiar creative elements connect the fun to the rights questions we will examine.
Before that, we need another distinction. Finding a fun combination and delivering a fully polished game are different achievements.

scenes.title: 재미와 완성도는 같은 점수가 아니다
lines: Early reactions include praise for how compelling it is, alongside criticism that some builds are too powerful or the difficulty is too low.
Balance, meaningful choices, and variety between runs each require examination. Adding many classes and skills does not automatically create deeper decisions.
Some reactions mention lag over longer sessions or problems with display and input. Those reports depend on the version and setup, and cannot be generalized to every current player.
In public comments, the creator acknowledged substantial work remained on difficulty and systems. We should not turn early reactions into a final verdict on quality.
It still matters that people can find it fun. A compelling growth-and-reward loop can work even while rough edges remain.
But a successful loop does not settle the rights to its artwork and sound. Let us move from evaluating fun to examining permission.

scenes.title: 무료 배포와 이용허락은 다르다
lines: Defeat monsters, gain experience, and level up. That sentence describes a rule for play. Copying a particular monster image into another game raises a different question.
The first concerns an idea for play; the second concerns the use of someone’s concrete expression. Music, animation, text, and software can matter as well as character art.

The U.S. Copyright Office explains that game ideas and methods of play are not themselves protected by copyright, while sufficiently creative artwork or writing may be. This U.S. guidance is not a universal legal verdict.

A 2019 Korean Supreme Court game decision adds an important consideration. It considers not only individual elements, but also their creative selection, arrangement, and combination into an overall expression.

Sharing the broad rule of a match-three puzzle differs from sharing a particular combination of characters, effects, progression, and presentation. That case involved Farm Heroes Saga and Forest Mania, not D2 Survivors.
We should avoid blanket claims that all rules may be copied freely, or that changing the pictures always makes it safe. The actual expression and specific rights require examination.

This distinction reveals a difference between our two examples. The Vampire Survivors interview describes a purchased, Castlevania-inspired asset pack. That is not evidence that original Castlevania graphics were directly taken.
Purchased assets still have permitted uses and conditions. But using an inspired asset pack and using another game’s actual files begin from different rights questions.

D2 Survivors’ current legal notice states that it is not approved by or affiliated with Blizzard. It also describes free access and a willingness to respond to rights holders, including taking the project down.
Free distribution describes the price charged, while permission concerns who authorized which use. A willingness to remove a project is not proof of prior authorization.
We also need to distinguish where files come from. The official guidance describes reading the user’s own Diablo II or Resurrected installation locally.

The legal notice also describes a temporary hosted copy during transition and an exception for subsets of Korean fonts. We therefore should not simplify the notice into a claim that every file necessarily comes only from the user’s computer.
Serving files to others and reading locally owned files can require different analysis. But buying a legitimate copy does not automatically authorize every use in another program.

This video is not an adjudication of D2 Survivors. We are separating observed gameplay, the developer’s statements, and the conditions needed for a legal judgment. That distinction also helps us read player reactions more accurately.

scenes.title: 같은 게임인데 반응이 갈리는 이유
lines: Some players first notice the experience of facing hordes with a nostalgic class. If it is fun and keeps them playing, they see a good game.
Others first ask whose work those familiar images and sounds represent. They question whether the use of another developer’s assets is justified.
Public comments include enjoyment, criticism of difficulty and polish, and objections to asset use. Different standards are being applied to the same game.
Discussion of Vampire Survivors and Magic Survival can show a similar divide. Some emphasize its debt to an earlier game, while others emphasize how genres develop by building on ideas.
A handful of comments does not represent all players. We must separate individual reactions from our interpretation of why people react that way.
Enjoyment does not answer a rights question, and a rights concern does not erase enjoyment. Different questions require different answers.

scenes.title: 팬게임이 남기는 가능성과 책임
lines: With those distinctions, we can go beyond blanket approval or rejection. Fan games can potentially offer new ways to experience old games and renew interest in the originals.
They can also reveal the combinations players want. Pairing familiar loot progression with compact survival combat is one example.
Those possibilities do not authorize every use of creative work. The artists, animators, composers, and sound creators still have work and rights involved.
On the other hand, treating every influence as identical copying makes it difficult to explain how games learn from one another. We need to identify both what was learned and what was actually used.

These are also practical questions for a developer. Are you recreating a principle of fun, or using someone else’s concrete assets? If it is the latter, have you checked the permission and conditions for that use?

scenes.title: 재미와 권리를 함께 보는 방법
lines: D2 Survivors invites us to examine why Diablo-style progression fits survivors-like combat. Vampire Survivors also built on earlier influences to create a distinct growth experience.
We should not collapse the two into one identical copyright issue. Influence on rules, similarity of expression, actual asset use, and permission each need examination.
We can acknowledge fun while asking about creators’ rights. We can also respect those rights while recognizing the importance of learning from existing games to create new experiences.
What if you had spent years developing the original game? Would you allow a fan project under conditions, ask it to replace the assets, or request that it stop using them?
Share the standards you would apply as a player and as a creator. This has been Yamyam Coding.
